newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: Fresh violence erupts in riot-torn French Guiana.
newsitem.headline: Fresh violence erupts in riot-torn French Guiana.

text.p: Fresh violence erupted late on Tuesday in the city of Cayenne in French Guiana when a magistrate's court convicted seven people arrested during riots last week, witnesses said.
At the announcement of the verdict, bands of youths began to overturn garbage cans. Riot police fired several rounds of tear gas to disperse the crowd, which had massed near the courthouse all day.

Two hundred paramilitary riot police reinforcements were flown in from Paris over the weekend to this French overseas territory in northeastern South America. They supplemented local police overwhelmed by the riots that killed one person, injured at least seven and caused millions of dollars of damage to government buildings and to stores on Thursday and Friday nights.
Airport officials told Reuters all incoming and outgoing flights at French Guiana's international airport near Cayenne would be cancelled on Wednesday.

The airport closure was triggered by a general strike called for Wednesday by an interunion group protesting against French government policy in French Guiana and the arrest of the seven rioters convicted on Tuesday.
High school students protesting against poor conditions in local schools sparked the riots when their strike degenerated into clashes between police and youths.
Earlier on Tuesday, the French government said in Paris it would hold wide-ranging talks next year on the situation in French Guiana.

Jean-Jacques de Peretti, minister of overseas territories, said he would visit Guiana shortly with Education Minister Francois Bayrou and organise a conference there next year, "because the future of the Guianese is a matter for the Guianese themselves."
De Peretti told the National Assembly that the problems of French Guiana stemmed largely from illegal immigration and a sharp increase in population to 140,000 from 80,000 over the past 13 years.

French Guiana is the only dependent territory in South America. Its economy lags behind that of mainland France, and it has an unemployment rate approaching 25 percent of the labour force. Joblessness is particularly acute among the young.
